content: Routine follow-up lumbar punctures to assess the response to antifungal treatment, such as cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) fungal cultures or cryptococcal antigen testing, are not recommended in lowand middle-income countries. This guidance is part of broader recommendations for diagnosing, preventing, and managing cryptococcal disease in HIV-infected adults, adolescents, and children. For individuals with persistent or recurrent symptoms, a structured diagnostic approach is advised to identify potential underlying causes. This includes reviewing the patient’s history for evidence of treatment failure due to inadequate drug regimens, poor adherence to fluconazole therapy, or drug resistance from prolonged fluconazole use. Paradoxical cryptococcal immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) should also be considered in patients who have started antiretroviral therapy (ART), after ruling out other causes of recurrent symptoms. Additionally, CSF should be sent or re-sent for prolonged fungal culture (incubated for two weeks). Other diseases with similar presentations, such as viral, bacterial, or tuberculous meningitis, should also be considered. Where possible, fluconazole susceptibility testing should be performed at a national reference laboratory in cases of suspected relapse despite adherence to fluconazole therapy. The increasing availability of ART has significantly improved the prognosis of people living with HIV in lowand middle-income countries, reducing HIV-related deaths by nearly 50% between 2005 and 2016. However, many individuals still present with advanced HIV disease, and opportunistic infections, such as cryptococcal disease, remain a major cause of mortality. Cryptococcal meningitis, the most common presentation of HIV-associated cryptococcal disease, accounts for 70–90% of cases and is responsible for a significant proportion of HIV-related deaths globally. In 2014, it was estimated to cause 223,100 cases and 181,100 deaths among people living with HIV, representing 15% of all HIV-related deaths worldwide. Mortality from cryptococcal meningitis is highest in low-income countries, with one-year mortality rates of 70% compared to 20–30% in high-income countries. A public health approach focusing on prevention, earlier diagnosis, and improved treatment of cryptococcal disease is critical to reducing its incidence and associated mortality in resource-limited settings. The World Health Organization (WHO) first published guidelines for the diagnosis, prevention, and management of cryptococcal disease in 2011. Since then, advances have been made, including evidence supporting the efficacy of cryptococcal antigen screening to identify individuals at risk, the use of short-course amphotericin B and flucytosine as induction therapy, and the superiority of flucytosine over fluconazole as a second-line drug in combination with amphotericin B. Recommendations also emphasize the importance of early ART initiation following a positive diagnosis and managing advanced HIV disease. The guidelines aim to provide evidence-based recommendations for preventing, diagnosing, and managing cryptococcal disease among adults, adolescents, and children living with HIV, particularly in resource-limited settings with a high burden of disease. They target HIV program managers, policymakers, healthcare professionals, and implementing partners in these settings. Key principles include adopting a public health approach to scaling up antiretroviral therapy (ART), emphasizing early ART initiation regardless of CD4 count, and ensuring prompt diagnosis and initiation of optimal antifungal treatment to improve survival and neurological outcomes. ART should be deferred by 4–6 weeks in cases of confirmed cryptococcal meningitis to prevent life-threatening IRIS in the central nervous system. Recommendations should be implemented based on local context, including HIV epidemiology, disease burden, access to diagnostic assays, and healthcare system capacity. Early diagnosis and treatment of cryptococcal meningitis are essential to reducing mortality. Healthcare professionals should maintain a high index of suspicion for cryptococcal meningitis in individuals with advanced HIV disease. In settings without access to lumbar puncture, rapid serum, plasma, or whole blood cryptococcal antigen assays are recommended. Screening for cryptococcal antigen followed by pre-emptive antifungal therapy is recommended for adults and adolescents with a CD4 count <100 cells/mm³ before initiating or reinitiating ART. This approach may also be considered for those with a CD4 count <200 cells/mm³. In settings where cryptococcal antigen screening is unavailable, fluconazole primary prophylaxis should be provided to individuals with a CD4 count <100 cells/mm³ and may be considered for those with a CD4 count <200 cells/mm³. Screening and prophylaxis are not recommended for children due to the low incidence of cryptococcal meningitis in this age group. The preferred treatment for cryptococcal meningitis in people living with HIV is one week of amphotericin B and flucytosine, followed by one week of fluconazole. Alternative induction regimens include two weeks of fluconazole and flucytosine or two weeks of amphotericin B and fluconazole. The consolidation phase involves fluconazole for eight weeks following induction therapy. Maintenance therapy with fluconazole is recommended to prevent relapse. Efforts to improve access to rapid diagnostic assays, antifungal drugs, and lumbar punctures are critical to reducing the high mortality associated with cryptococcal meningitis in lowand middle-income countries. Further research is needed to evaluate the cost-effectiveness of screening at higher CD4 thresholds, the value of cryptococcal antigen screening in ART-experienced individuals, and the feasibility of using blood antigen titers to guide management in settings where lumbar puncture is not feasible.
